title: Out of Memory Error: Failed to allocate block of 13230080 bytes
body:
### What happens?

I am performing the following query with a window function and `QUALIFY` clause on a GCP `n2-highmem-64` instance (64 CPU, 500GB RAM, with plenty of free swap just in case).

```sql
-- perform query
CREATE TABLE tbl_out AS
SELECT
	A, B, C,
	row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY A, B ORDER BY C DESC) AS D
FROM tbl_in
QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY A, B ORDER BY C DESC) <= 5
ORDER BY A, B, D ASC;
```

DuckDB is configured as such:

```sql
-- only use 16 threads and 200G RAM, set a temporary directory
SET threads TO 16;
SET memory_limit = '200GB';
SET temp_directory='<some path>';
```

This issue is likely similar to https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/issues/8135: the issue happens randomly, and there's 300GB of free RAM available.

As advised by @participant2 [here](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/issues/8135#issuecomment-1684399615), I reduced the thread count which helped for previous queries, but not this one. I set memory to less than 50% of the available RAM. I set up a temporary directory.

This query works on my OSX M1 Max, 64GB RAM, 10 CPUs.

### To Reproduce

I cannot share the original data as it is private, but I generated synthetic data that keeps the original cardinality and reproduce the error.

On a GCP instance `n2-highmem-64`,

```bash
$ curl -O https://storage.googleapis.com/capp-dev/duckdb/tbl_in.parquet
$ duckdb oom
```

then

```sql
SET threads TO 16;
SET memory_limit = '200GB';
SET temp_directory='tmp';

CREATE TABLE tbl_in AS SELECT * FROM 'tbl_in.parquet';

CREATE TABLE tbl_out AS
SELECT
	A, B, C,
	row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY A, B ORDER BY C DESC) AS D
FROM tbl_in
QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY A, B ORDER BY C DESC) <= 5
ORDER BY A, B, D ASC;
```

You should likely see the following error:

```
Out of Memory Error: Failed to allocate block of XXXX bytes
```

although you have plenty of free RAM

### OS:

Linux instance-2 5.10.0-26-cloud-amd64 #1 SMP Debian 5.10.197-1 (2023-09-29) x86_64 GNU/Linux

### DuckDB Version:

0.9.2

### DuckDB Client:

CLI & Go

### Full Name:

Gawen Arab

### Affiliation:

airbuds.fm

### Have you tried this on the latest `main` branch?

I have tested with a release build (and could not test with a main build)

### Have you tried the steps to reproduce? Do they include all relevant data and configuration? Does the issue you report still appear there?

- [X] Yes, I have

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
The data has ~1B rows of ~50 bytes each, giving an uncompressed size of ~50GB.  Parquet (and DuckDB) do an admirable job of compressing this data (3.8GB for DuckDB and 1.2GB for parquet). 

When we partition, we have no compression, and the partitions leave empty space to avoid reallocation overhead, so the partitions will end up being a significant multiple of this uncompressed size. With 16 threads, the data will be split into ~16M rows per thread, each of which has 1024 partition buffers. These buffers will then each end up containing ~16K rows of _uncompressed_ data, along with what appears to be an average of 50% buffering overhead, for an average row cost of ~100GB.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
One workaround is to compress the strings yourself:

```sql
create temporary table dim_a as 
    select row_number() over (order by A) AS aid, A 
    from (select distinct A from tbl_in order by all) t;

create temporary table dim_b as 
    select row_number() over (order by B) AS bid, B 
    from (select distinct B from tbl_in order by all) t;

WITH view_in as (
    select 
    	aid::INTEGER as A, 
    	bid::TINYINT as B, 
    	C 
    from tbl_in, dim_a, dim_b 
    where tbl_in.A = dim_a.A 
      and tbl_in.B = dim_b.B
)
SELECT
	A, B, C,
	row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY A, B ORDER BY C DESC) AS D
FROM view_in
QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY A, B ORDER BY C DESC) <= 5
ORDER BY A, B, D ASC;
```

This completes for me in about a minute using < 50GB on 16 cores.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body: Another part of the problem is that the strings are too long to inline (> 12 bytes) so we have to allocate heap blocks instead of treating them as fixed-width data.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Thanks @participant2 for the investigation, the insights about how it works internally, and your advice to optimize it! 🙏 

I'd like to clarify my understanding of the issue we're addressing. Is your objective to reduce the memory usage of this query to make it work? It seems that the main problem isn't that duckdb is running out of available RAM; in fact, it sometimes raises an OOM error when allocating few KiB blocks of memory, despite there are GiBs of RAM unused. This occurs regardless of setting the `memory_limit` to a high percentage of the available RAM.

This lead me to the conclusion that the root issue is closely tied to the memory allocator being `jemalloc` rather than the query's memory usage itself. Maybe some memory fragmentation, or some configuration limit to fine-tune 💭. Disabling `jemalloc` makes it work all the time without any OOMs. WDYT?

> The data has ~1B rows of ~50 bytes each,
> [...]
> Another part of the problem is that the strings are too long to inline (> 12 bytes) so we have to allocate heap blocks instead of treating them as fixed-width data.

Note that the dataset in `tbl_in` is synthetic and only matches the original dataset's `approx_unique`s. Rows and string lengths were changed.

Thanks again for your time!

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
Good question. My objective was actually to see if there was something dumb going on in the window operator (which is my responsibility). The workaround came from my observations of that. 

But why the allocator is failing is something I have little clue about and should probably be addressed by another member of the team. I do know that not all of our memory is tracked, which can be an issue at times. it may also be that once the partitioning ground through, we were unable to allocate a large untracked block of 1/1024 of the data for the window calculations on one of the cores.

comments.author: participant15
comments.body:
> I have fixed my OOM issue by disabling `jemalloc` on Ubuntu, just run this `GEN=ninja BUILD_JSON=1 SKIP_EXTENSIONS=jemalloc BUILD_JEMALLOC=0 make`

This worked for me!

Alternatively, another option that worked for me was tuning the `jemalloc` parameters by declaring an environment variable `MALLOC_CONF`. This was after `pip install duckdb` so latest version (1.0.0)

```
export MALLOC_CONF="narenas:8,lg_chunk:21,background_thread:true,dirty_decay_ms:1000,muzzy_decay_ms:10000"
```

or if you want to set it in your python code:

```python
os.environ["MALLOC_CONF"] = (
    f"narenas:{os.cpu_count()},lg_chunk:21,background_thread:true,dirty_decay_ms:10000,muzzy_decay_ms:10000"
)
```

I just set `narenas` to CPU count. If memory is not an issue, this should be fine.

Here are some commonly used jemalloc options that you might find useful:

 - narenas: Sets the number of arenas. More arenas can reduce contention in multi-threaded applications but may increase memory usage.
 - lg_chunk: Sets the chunk size. Larger chunks can reduce fragmentation but may increase memory usage.
dirty_decay_ms: Controls the time (in milliseconds) before dirty pages are purged. Lower values can reduce memory usage at the cost of performance.
 - muzzy_decay_ms: Similar to dirty_decay_ms, but for "muzzy" pages (pages that have been decommitted but not yet purged).
 - background_thread: Enables or disables background threads for purging unused memory. Setting this to true can improve performance by offloading purging work to background threads.

> I just set `narenas` to CPU count. If memory is not an issue, this should be fine.
> 
> Here are some commonly used jemalloc options that you might find useful:
> 
> * narenas: Sets the number of arenas. More arenas can reduce contention in multi-threaded applications but may increase memory usage.
> * lg_chunk: Sets the chunk size. Larger chunks can reduce fragmentation but may increase memory usage.
>   dirty_decay_ms: Controls the time (in milliseconds) before dirty pages are purged. Lower values can reduce memory usage at the cost of performance.
> * muzzy_decay_ms: Similar to dirty_decay_ms, but for "muzzy" pages (pages that have been decommitted but not yet purged).
> * background_thread: Enables or disables background threads for purging unused memory. Setting this to true can improve performance by offloading purging work to background threads.

this doesn't seem to work on my mac.
I was trying to convert a 13GB JSONL file into a temporary table using:

```sql
CREATE TEMP TABLE tmp_tb AS (
  SELECT 
    *,
    row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY A) AS row_number
  FROM read_json('13G_file.jsonl', union_by_name=True)
)
```

with config 

```sql
SET threads = 10;
SET memory_limit = '5GB';
```

But it consistently failed until I increased the memory limit.

The tricky part is that success appears to depend on the following relationship:

```
memory_limit = 0.08 × file_size_GB × threads
```

For example, with `threads = 10`, I needed to set the memory limit to at least `10.4GB`.
If I want to cap memory usage at `6GB`, I need to keep the number of threads under `5`.

Is this expected? For a 1TB file with 10 threads, would I really need at least 819GB of memory?

It's happening with the Splink python package when using duckdb as the backend: https://github.com/moj-analytical-services/splink/discussions/2752

Alot of reproducing the error is dependant on the model in Splink as well as the input dataset which I cannot provide, but I'll try and give a few details.

- If I use newer versions of duckdb above v1.0.0, the RAM that duckdb uses is never relased back for the Python process to continue using
- With duckdb v1.0.0, memory for one part of the model process is released back, but in another process, it starts spilling ~500+GB to disk (the input dataset is only a 300mb parquet file).
